passages.t: A person vowed to the LORD
passages.happening:
The LORD speaks of the time “When someone makes a special vow to the LORD involving the value of persons” (verse 2). A sum in silver is set for each case.

For a man from twenty to sixty years old it is fifty shekels, and for a woman thirty (verses 3-4). From five to twenty, twenty shekels for a male and ten for a female (verse 5). From a month to five years, five and three (verse 6). From sixty upward, fifteen and ten (verse 7).

“But if the one making the vow is too poor to pay the valuation, he is to present the person before the priest, who shall set the value according to what the one making the vow can afford” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 26 ended like the close of a book. This chapter follows as an appendix, with its own last line. After blessings and curses for a whole nation, Leviticus ends quietly, with what one ordinary person might promise to God.

A vow was a promise made to God, often in trouble: if you bring me through this, I will give you this. People in the Bible vowed a tenth of their goods, an offering, and sometimes a person, themselves or a child.

A person vowed to God could not go and serve in the tent. Only the tribe of Levi did that. So the vow was kept by paying the person's value in silver to the sanctuary. This passage sets the sums.

These were large amounts for an ordinary family. Joseph's brothers sold him for twenty shekels, the sum set here for a boy of his age.

The last verse of the passage is the kind one. The poor were not shut out of making a vow. The priest set a price to match what the person could pay. It is the same mercy the book has shown before, with birds in place of a lamb.
passages.later:
Hannah made such a vow when she prayed for a son: “then I will dedicate him to the LORD all the days of his life” (1 Samuel 1:11). She kept it, and Samuel grew up at the sanctuary.

Jacob vowed a tenth at Bethel: “of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth” (Genesis 28:22).

The wisdom writers were cautious about vows: “It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it” (Ecclesiastes 5:5).
passages.hard:
Why is a man valued at more than a woman, and an adult at more than a child or an old person?

The different sums can look like a ranking of human worth, and a modern reader is right to ask.

Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, understand the figures as a measure of work. They reflect what a person's labor would have been worth to the sanctuary in a farming economy. They do not measure a person's value before God. That is why the years of full strength are set highest, and why a man over sixty is set lower than a woman in her working years.

Others add that the figures still reflect a world in which women's work was counted for less, and that the text records that world without endorsing it as God's view of people. Both points can be true.

The rest of Scripture is plain. Every human being is made in the image of God: “male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). And Paul writes that in Christ “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female” (Galatians 3:28).

No one's worth is a sum of money. No child, no old person, no one who can no longer work is worth less to God.
passages.asks: The priest set the price by what a poor person could pay, so that no one was kept from giving. Ask whether you have held back from giving to God because what you have seems too small. And ask whether you measure people, yourself included, by what they can produce.

passages.happening:
An animal that can be offered, once vowed, is holy. “He must not replace it or exchange it, either good for bad or bad for good” (verse 10). If he tries, both animals are holy.

An unclean animal, a house or a field can be vowed and then bought back. The priest sets its value, and the owner who wants it back “must add a fifth to its value” (verses 13, 15, 19).

A field is valued by the seed it takes and by the years left until the Jubilee (verses 16-18). “Every valuation will be according to the sanctuary shekel” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The chapter now goes through the things a person might give: an animal, a house, a piece of land.

Two rules stand out.

No swapping. A person who has promised God a good animal may not quietly put a poorer one in its place. The law even forbids swapping a bad one for a good one. What has been given to God is his, and the giver does not manage it any more. Anyone who tries ends up giving both.

And an added fifth. Someone who gives a house or field and then wants it back may have it, at its value and a fifth more. The extra made people think before they vowed, and think again before they took a gift back.

The Jubilee of chapter 25 is at work here too. A field could not be given away for ever, because it would return to its family in the fiftieth year. So its value was reckoned by the harvests left.

The word ‘valuation’ comes twenty-one times in the chapter. It is a practical, careful law. A promise to God was a serious matter, and it was to be kept honestly.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy says of vows, “Be careful to follow through on what comes from your lips, because you have freely vowed to the LORD your God with your own mouth” (Deuteronomy 23:23). It also says that a person who makes no vow has done nothing wrong (Deuteronomy 23:22).

Jesus rebuked a misuse of vows in his own day. Some declared their goods ‘Corban’, given to God, so as not to have to support their parents. He said, “Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down” (Mark 7:13).

He also taught his followers to be people whose plain word can be trusted: “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37).
passages.asks: What was promised to God could not be quietly swapped for something cheaper. Ask what you once promised God, in a crisis or in gratitude, and whether you kept it. And ask whether your yes can be relied on, by God and by the people around you.

passages.happening:
“But no one may consecrate a firstborn of the livestock, because a firstborn belongs to the LORD” (verse 26).

Anything a person has devoted to the LORD without condition cannot be sold or bought back: “everything so devoted is most holy to the LORD” (verse 28). Verse 29 says that a person set apart for destruction may not be ransomed.

“Thus any tithe from the land, whether from the seed of the land or the fruit of the trees, belongs to the LORD; it is holy to the LORD” (verse 30). Every tenth animal that passes under the shepherd's rod is the LORD's, and the owner may not pick and choose (verses 32-33).

“These are the commandments that the LORD gave to Moses for the Israelites on Mount Sinai” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The last part of the book is about things that cannot be vowed, because they are God's already.

The firstborn of the animals belonged to God from the night of the exodus. A person cannot make a gift of what he already owes.

The tithe, the tenth of crop and herd, is the same. It is not presented here as a generous extra. It ‘belongs to the LORD’. The tenth animal was counted off as the flock passed under the shepherd's staff, one by one, with no looking to see whether it was a good one. The owner could not keep the best back.

Between these comes a harder category. The Hebrew is cherem, something given over to God completely and beyond recall. It could never be bought back. Verse 29 applies this to a person. It most likely means someone already condemned to death under the law, or in the wars of the conquest, whose sentence could not be bought off with money. It is not a licence for anyone to vow another person's death, and it is no pattern for anyone today.

Then the last line. The whole book is gathered under one heading: commandments given at Sinai. Leviticus began with God calling from the tent to a people who could not come in. It ends with those people taught how to bring their offerings, their bodies, their meals, their fields, their time and their promises to him. The thought that runs under this last chapter runs under the whole book: everything already belongs to God, and a holy life is one that treats it so.
passages.later:
The firstborn were claimed at the exodus: “Consecrate to Me every firstborn male” (Exodus 13:2).

God gave the tithes to the tribe that had no land: “I have given to the Levites all the tithes in Israel as an inheritance in return for the work they do” (Numbers 18:21).

Jesus did not dismiss the tithe, but he would not let it stand in for greater things. Of teachers who tithed their garden herbs he said, “you have disregarded the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness. You should have practiced the latter, without neglecting the former” (Matthew 23:23).

Paul takes the book's language of belonging and gives it to Christians: “You are not your own; you were bought at a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).
passages.hard:
Must Christians tithe?

Christians differ. Some hold that the tenth is a standing rule for God's people, older than Sinai, since Abraham and Jacob gave it. Others hold that the tithe belonged to the law of Moses, with its Levites and its sanctuary, and that the New Testament sets no figure but calls for giving that is free, generous and glad: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Many who take the second view still treat a tenth as a wise place to begin. These notes take no side.

On one thing there is no room for doubt. No one may use this chapter to press money out of people who cannot afford it, or to promise that God will pay them back. If you gave money because you were pressed or frightened, or because someone promised that God would pay you back, and the return never came, that was not your failure. You were not lacking in faith. The promise was wrong. It may help to talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If you are in money trouble now, look for a trusted adviser where you live; these notes are not financial advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The book ends by saying that the first and the tenth are God's already. Ask what in your life you treat as wholly yours that was only ever on loan. And look back over Leviticus: ask what it would mean for your meals, your money, your body, your time and your word all to be holy to the LORD.
